blocks.content: By default, a port a process listens on inside a container is not reachable from outside the host at all. Port mapping, via the -p flag, is what deliberately opens a path from a host port to a container port.
1. Container Ports Are Isolated by Default
blocks.text: 1. Container Ports Are Isolated by Default

blocks.content: Even if nginx inside a container is listening on port 80, nothing outside that container, not your browser, not another machine, can reach it unless you explicitly map it. This isolation is a direct consequence of the container having its own network namespace.

blocks.alt: A listening port inside is invisible from outside, by default

blocks.content: -p hostPort:containerPort tells Docker to forward traffic arriving on a specific host port through to a specific port inside the container. Once mapped, anything that can reach the host on that port can reach the container's service.

blocks.alt: Host port forwards straight through to the container port

blocks.content:
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
# Host port 8080 now forwards to the container's port 80.
# curl http://localhost:8080 now reaches nginx inside it.

code.content:
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
# Host port 8080 now forwards to the container's port 80.
# curl http://localhost:8080 now reaches nginx inside it.

codes.bash:
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
# Host port 8080 now forwards to the container's port 80.
# curl http://localhost:8080 now reaches nginx inside it.

blocks.content: A single docker run can map as many ports as needed, one -p flag per mapping, useful when a container exposes more than one service or you are juggling several containers that each need their own host-facing port.

docker run -d -p 8080:80 -p 8443:443 mywebapp
docker run -d -p 5432:5432 postgres

code.content:
docker run -d -p 8080:80 -p 8443:443 mywebapp
docker run -d -p 5432:5432 postgres

codes.bash:
docker run -d -p 8080:80 -p 8443:443 mywebapp
docker run -d -p 5432:5432 postgres

blocks.content: 4. Container-to-Container Traffic Does Not Need This
blocks.text: 4. Container-to-Container Traffic Does Not Need This

blocks.content: Port mapping only matters for traffic coming from outside the Docker network, from your host or the internet. Two containers on the same Docker network can already reach each other directly by container name and internal port, no -p mapping required at all (the full mechanics are covered in the Docker Networking module).

blocks.alt: Containers on the same network talk directly, no mapping needed

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A container's ports are unreachable from outside the host by default, -p hostPort:containerPort is what deliberately opens that path.
Port mapping is only for external access, containers on the same Docker network can already reach each other directly without it.
